A missing cell, a stopped cell, a container that is not Attachable, or a container whose task is not running fail with the same errors as kuke attach, and nothing is written. Input that cannot be expanded (a dangling ^, ^!, \n, a short \x) fails before any connection is made.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Type a command and press Enter
kuke write mycell "echo hello^M"

# Interrupt the foreground program
kuke write mycell "^C"

# Type without submitting, check the screen, then submit
kuke write mycell "rm -rf build"
kuke screenshot mycell
kuke write mycell "^M"

# From stdin
printf 'make test^M' | kuke write mycell -

# Verbatim bytes
kuke write mycell --raw "$(printf 'ls\r')"

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• kuke screenshot — see the terminal's screen
  • kuke attach — interactive terminal

docs.title: kuke (root)
docs.text:
kuke [global flags] <subcommand> [args]

The kuke binary is the client CLI. It parses flags, opens a connection to kukeond, sends a request, and formats the response.

docs.title: Persistent flags
docs.text: These flags apply to every kuke subcommand. Defaults are shown in parentheses.

docs.title: --run-path (/opt/kukeon)
docs.text: Where Kukeon stores on-disk metadata for realms, spaces, stacks, cells, and containers. Must be writable by the process running kuke — typically root, or a member of the kukeon group when talking to the daemon over its group-readable socket.

docs.title: --configuration ($HOME/.kuke/kuke.yaml)
docs.text: Path to a ClientConfiguration YAML. If the file doesn't exist, Kukeon falls back to command-line flags, environment variables, and hardcoded defaults — a missing config file is not fatal.

docs.title: --containerd-socket (/run/containerd/containerd.sock)
docs.text: Path to the containerd socket. Only used when running in in-process mode; when talking to the daemon, containerd is accessed by the daemon, not the client.

docs.title: --host (unix:///run/kukeon/kukeond.sock)
docs.text: The daemon endpoint. Today only the unix:// scheme is supported. The ssh://user@host scheme is reserved for a future remote-management feature; don't use it yet.

docs.title: --no-daemon (only on init / uninstall / purge / get <kind>)
docs.text:
Bypass kukeond and run the operation in-process. Requires root: the client now directly touches containerd, CNI, and cgroups.

--no-daemon is not a root-persistent flag — it is only accepted on kuke init, kuke uninstall, kuke purge, and every kuke get <kind> (see #222; the get kinds were retained per a user override on the original AC so the in-process escape hatch stays available for every resource lookup, not just get realm). For the other promotable callers that don't carry the flag — log, refresh, restart, start, stop, doctor cgroups — reach the in-process path via KUKEON_NO_DAEMON=true in the environment or via an explicit --run-path /path (which auto-promotes to in-process mode so a caller-supplied run-path is never silently sent to the wrong daemon). The true workload verbs (apply, create *, run, attach, delete *, kill *) route through the daemon-only client after #566/#588: they ignore kukeon/noDaemon, so neither KUKEON_NO_DAEMON=true nor --run-path promotes them — they always require the daemon.

kuke image * is daemon-independent by design and is always in-process regardless of any of these knobs.

Don't run two in-process commands at the same time — they'll race on the same on-disk state.

In-process start, stop, refresh and purge are not serialised against a running kukeond: the per-cell lock that orders the daemon's lifecycle verbs against its reconcile tick is an in-process mutex, not a file lock, so it does not reach a second process (#1569). Use the in-process path for these verbs only while the daemon is stopped — it is the escape hatch for when the daemon is down, not a second way to drive a live one.

docs.title: --verbose, -v (false)
docs.text: Turn on structured slog output to stderr. Pair with --log-level debug for the chattiest view.

docs.title: --log-level (info)
docs.text: One of debug, info, warn, error. Controls log verbosity when --verbose is set.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Every flag also has a corresponding KUKE_* environment variable (check via --help on a subcommand, or see cmd/config/env.go). Flags beat env vars beat the config file beats built-in defaults.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Talk to a non-default socket
kuke --host unix:///tmp/kukeond.sock get realms

# Bypass the daemon (in-process via env var) — surviving promotable callers only
sudo KUKEON_NO_DAEMON=true kuke get cells --realm default --space default --stack default

# Bypass the daemon (in-process via --run-path promotion)
sudo kuke purge realm myrealm --cascade --force --run-path /opt/kukeon

# Verbose debug of a single apply
sudo kuke apply -f cell.yaml --verbose --log-level debug

docs.title: Subcommands
docs.text: See Commands overview for the list.

docs.title: kukeond
docs.text:
The daemon binary. Normally you don't run kukeond by hand — it runs as the root container of the kukeond cell in the system realm, under containerd. Running it directly is useful when you want to run the daemon on the host without wrapping it in a container (for example, in a CI job or during deep debugging).

kukeond serve [flags]

docs.title: Persistent flags
docs.text:
Flag Default Description --socket /run/kukeon/kukeond.sock Unix socket the daemon listens on --socket-gid 0 Group ID to chown the listener socket to (mode 0660 with group). Set by kuke init to the kukeon GID. --run-path /opt/kukeon Where the daemon reads/writes persistent state (shared with kuke) --containerd-socket /run/containerd/containerd.sock Path to the containerd socket --configuration /etc/kukeon/kukeond.yaml ServerConfiguration YAML; absent file uses hardcoded defaults --cgroup-root /kukeon Cgroup root under which all realms / spaces / stacks / cells live --containerd-namespace-suffix kukeon.io Suffix appended to every realm name to form its containerd namespace --reconcile-interval 30s Period of the cell-reconciliation loop (Go duration; 0 disables) --log-level info Log level: debug, info, warn, error

kukeond's --run-path matches kuke's default — both binaries share the same /opt/kukeon tree. The socket and pid files live under /run/kukeon and are controlled by --socket independently.

docs.title: kukeond serve
docs.text:
kukeond serve

Runs the daemon in the foreground. Listens on --socket, writes a pid file at /run/kukeon/kukeond.pid, and serves the kukeonv1 API until it receives SIGINT or SIGTERM.

On shutdown it closes the listener, removes the pid file, and drains in-flight requests on a best-effort basis.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
sudo kukeond serve --log-level debug

This runs the daemon on the host directly. In the normal path, kuke init creates a cell for it and containerd starts the container for you — see System realm.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
• SIGINT, SIGTERM — clean shutdown.
  • SIGKILL — hard kill; leaves the socket and pid file behind. Clean up with sudo rm -f /run/kukeon/kukeond.{sock,pid} before restarting (or use kuke daemon reset).

docs.title: Blueprint contract: components and modes
docs.text:
A blueprint is a form; a config is the answers.

A CellBlueprint describes a kind of cell and everything that may differ between two cells of that kind. A CellConfig answers it for one use. Because the blueprint is self-describing — typed parameters, named slots, components, modes, required image capabilities — anything can build a Config for it without knowing the template body: kuke team does, and so does the web UI's New config form.

The blueprint fixes The config answers The cell template: containers, commands, mounts, privileges values for the typed parameters Which parameters exist, their type, default and form group repos — a URL and revision per repo slot Which repo and secret slots exist and which are required secrets — a stored Secret per secret slot The components it is assembled from and the modes a harness starts in components to enable, modes to allow, extra requires The image capabilities it needs git — an override of the inherited git identity

Security posture stays in the blueprint. Running as root, privileged mode and host mounts are never a Config toggle: each posture is its own blueprint (claude, claude-root, …), so choosing one is a visible choice of blueprint.

Git identity and credentials are never in the blueprint either. A default identity is inherited from the Realm, Space or Stack (or set on the Config), and any repo may state its own.

docs.title: Typed parameters
docs.text: Every ${KEY} the template references can be declared with a type — string, enum, path, image, bool — an enum list, a default, a description and a group. The daemon rejects a value that does not fit its type when it renders a cell; a form uses the same declarations to draw the right input and to group fields.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
A component bundles one concern:

  • harness — the agent harness: its env, parameters, secret slots and the modes it can be started in.
  • connector — access to an external service through that service's API credentials. The GitHub connector delivers a token as GH_TOKEN for the gh CLI.
  • forge — the issue/change tracker the cell works against.

A component that is not optional is always part of the cell. An optional one is included only when the Config lists it in spec.components. When the daemon renders a cell it flattens the enabled components into the template: their parameters join the blueprint's, their env and secret slots land on one container, and their requires join the cell's. Two enabled components (or a component and the template) that claim the same env key or secret destination fail the render rather than silently overriding each other.

A component never contributes a git credential. That is deliberate: the GitHub connector's token is for the GitHub API; clone, fetch, push and signing use only the cell's git identity. An API token in the environment can therefore never take over a push.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
A harness usually starts in more than one way. Its component declares them as modes:

  • interactive — an attachable session. No prompt; a login typically persists in a state volume.
  • headless — a dispatched, unattended run. It takes what an unattended run needs: a PROMPT parameter, possibly an API-key secret, its own entrypoint.

Each mode carries its own onInit, parameters, env and secrets, and everything it declares applies only to cells created in that mode. A Config says which modes are allowed and which is the default; the mode itself is picked per cell, at create time:

kuke run dev-claude                                           # the config's default mode
kuke run dev-claude --mode headless --param PROMPT="fix the build" -d

So one Config serves both an attached cell and a dispatched run. --param on a Config-sourced cell is accepted only for the picked mode's parameters — a Config's own values are not overridable per cell. A cell that supplies a parameter only one mode declares is created in that mode without --mode (--param PROMPT=…, or --env PROMPT=… as dispatches were written before modes existed).

The mode is recorded on the cell (kukeon.io/mode label and the cell's provenance), so a restart or an OutOfSync re-render keeps it.

docs.title: Image capabilities
docs.text:
A cell needs an image that actually contains what it is going to run. The requirement is

blueprint requires  ∪  enabled components' requires  ∪  config requires

and images declare what they provide in the OCI image label io.kukeon.capabilities — a comma-separated list such as claude,git,gh,go,node,make. The harness images kukeon publishes are stamped with it at build, from harness.yaml images[].capabilities.

When a cell is created the daemon reads the label of each container image and refuses an image that declares capabilities but lacks a required one, naming the missing capability. An image with no label at all is allowed with a warning, so images built before the label existed — and images you build yourself — keep working. The web UI filters its image picker on the same label.

docs.title: Shared blueprints
docs.text: A blueprint without role facts can be shared. kuke team renders one blueprint per harness × security profile, realm-wide (claude, claude-root, codex, …), labelled kukeon.io/shared: "true", and every role's Config in the realm references it. See Team.

docs.title: Cell
docs.text:
A cell is a pod-like unit: a group of containers that share a network namespace. Exactly one container in each cell is the root container — it owns the network namespace, and every other container in the cell joins it.

If you've worked with Kubernetes pods, the mental model is the same. One pause-like container would have held the network namespace; in Kukeon, one of your actual containers is marked as the root.

docs.title: What a cell is
docs.text:
Creating a cell materializes:

  1. A cgroup subtree — /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/<realm>/<space>/<stack>/<cell> — parent of every container in the cell.
  2. A Linux network namespace, entered by the root container and shared by the rest.
  3. A veth pair between the cell's network namespace and the space's bridge, configured by the CNI bridge plugin and host-local IPAM.
  4. Metadata at /opt/kukeon/<realm>/<space>/<stack>/<cell>/cell.yaml.

docs.title: Cell spec
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Cell
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  id: web
  realmId: main
  spaceId: default
  stackId: default
  containers:
    - id: nginx
      image: docker.io/library/nginx:alpine
      root: true # owns the network namespace
    - id: sidecar
      image: docker.io/library/busybox:latest
      command: /bin/sh
      args: ["-c", "while true; do date; sleep 5; done"]

See Manifest Reference → Cell for the full schema.

docs.title: Identity, lineage, and provenance
docs.text:
A cell's identity is its own document — the CellDoc. The CellDoc owns the cell's metadata.name, its spec (containers, scope, volumes, …), and its status. Nothing outside the cell owns its name: a cell materialized from a CellBlueprint or CellConfig gets a fresh <prefix>-<6hex> name (or a --name-pinned one), and the binding it came from is recorded as lineage, not identity.

  • Lineage labels. A cell stamped from a binding carries a back-reference label — kukeon.io/config=<name> for a Config-lineage cell, kukeon.io/blueprint=<name> for a Blueprint-lineage one. These are 1:N back-references (a binding stamps N cells), used to list a binding's cells (kuke get cells -l kukeon.io/config=<name>) and to drive the daemon's OutOfSync reconcile — not to pin a singleton.
  • Materialization provenance. Each stamped cell also persists a Spec.Provenance block — the binding kind, its scoped ref, the resolved params, and any per-cell --env and --connector overrides — so kuke restart <cell> can re-resolve the cell from its binding without re-supplying values.
  • Clone provenance. A cell forked with kuke run --clone <cell> / kuke create cell --clone <cell> carries the kukeon.io/source-cell=<name> annotation recording the cell it was forked from. Unlike the lineage labels it is inert debug/grooming metadata: no reconcile or selector path keys off it, and it pins no identity. The clone keeps the source's lineage label and provenance binding, so it re-resolves against the same Blueprint/Config the source did.

docs.title: The root container
docs.text:
• One container in a cell must be the root. If none is set explicitly, the first container declared is chosen.
  • The root container is created first. Its network namespace is the cell's network namespace.
  • Non-root containers join the same network namespace at creation time.
  • The root anchors the cell: workloads join its network, IPC and UTS namespaces, kukeon reaches the cell's network through the root's PID, and the cell's CNI/IPAM lease is keyed to the root container. It must stay alive for as long as any workload runs.
  • When every workload has finished, the reconciler stops the root (see Lifecycle), whatever the workloads' restartPolicy.
  • When the root container exits while a workload is still running, the reconciler kills the remaining workloads, releases the cell's network, and settles the cell in Error with reason RootContainerExited. Cells with only a root container (kukeond-style) are different: there the root is the workload, and the cell's state follows the root.

docs.title: Cell networking
docs.text:
• One IP per cell, not per container. All containers in the cell share the network namespace and therefore share the IP.
  • localhost in any container reaches every port bound by every container in the same cell.
  • The cell's IP is assigned by the space's CNI configuration (by default, from the bridge plugin's host-local range).
  • Two cells in the same space can reach each other at the IP layer; two cells in different spaces cannot (unless you join them into a shared network).

docs.title: States
docs.text: State What it means Pending The cell's status was never written by a lifecycle path. kuke create cell stamps Stopped, so a cell is not normally seen in Pending today. start, run <cell> and restart refuse it; delete it and create it again. Ready The workloads are running. For a root-only cell, the root is running. Degraded Some workloads are running, but at least one is down in a non-clean way: it crashed, or it exited under a restartPolicy that wants it running and the reconciler is restarting it (or waiting out its backoff). Not sticky: the reconciler re-derives it every pass, so it returns to Ready when the workload recovers and settles to Error once an on-failure workload exhausts its retry cap. Stopped The operator stopped the cell (kuke stop / kuke kill), or kuke create cell materialized it without starting it. Only those paths set it; the reconciler never derives it. When an operator stop interrupts a cell that had not finished (a workload was running, the cell was Degraded, or a restart was owed), the cell also carries reason OperatorStopped, and the label is durable: the reconciler keeps it Stopped across passes. Exited Every workload exited 0 on its own, and no restart is owed. Auto-delete-eligible: a kuke run --rm cell in this state is deleted. Error A workload exited non-zero and no restart is owed (reason WorkloadFailed), or the root died under running workloads (reason RootContainerExited). message names the container and its exit code or signal. Sticky: the reconciler does not re-derive it, and it is never auto-deleted, so the failure stays inspectable. It is still restartable: kuke start / run <cell> / restart recreate the cell. Failed A kukeon bring-up fault: create, start or recreate failed. A crashed workload is Error, not Failed. Sticky like Error, and restartable the same way. Unknown kukeon cannot tell (for example containerd is unreachable, or a workload's task status could not be read). The reconciler waits for the next pass rather than act on it.

docs.title: Exits, wind-down and root death
docs.text:
Each reconcile pass reads every container's task from containerd and applies these rules, in order:

  1. Sticky states are kept. Error and Failed are not re-derived. An Error cell whose root is still running is wound down (see rule 5) and keeps its label.
  2. A durable Stopped is kept. A never-started cell, or one carrying OperatorStopped, stays Stopped unless a workload is seen running again (a task started outside kukeon).
  3. Root death. If the root is terminal while a workload is still running, the reconciler kills every workload, runs the CNI/IPAM cleanup, and sets Error with reason RootContainerExited in the same pass. An Unknown root read does not count. Root-only cells are exempt.
  4. Derivation and restarts. For a cell with workloads, the state follows the workloads, not the root: Ready if they are all up, Degraded if some are up and one is down, Exited if all exited 0, Error if any exited non-zero. A root-only cell follows its root. A workload whose restartPolicy asks for a restart (always on any exit, on-failure on a non-zero exit) is restarted, subject to its backoff and retry cap; while a restart is owed the cell is held at Degraded. restartPolicy decides only whether a workload is restarted.
  5. Wind-down. Once every workload is terminal and no restart is owed (derived Exited or Error), the reconciler stops the root within that pass, whatever the restartPolicy. The stop is graceful: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 5 seconds. A root that handles SIGTERM, such as the injected kukepause root, ends with exit 0; one that ignores it (for example sleep infinity as PID 1) ends with exit 137. Every container's task is deleted, so every container then reads Stopped with its last exit code preserved. The cell keeps its derived Exited / Error label and its reason / message; it never passes through Stopped. Container records and snapshots stay, so the cell can be started again.
  6. --rm. A cell with spec.autoDelete (kuke run --rm) that settles Exited is killed and deleted instead of wound down. Error, Failed and OperatorStopped cells are never auto-deleted.

kuke refresh applies rules 1, 2 and 4 the same way but acts on nothing: it never restarts, winds down, tears down or deletes a cell.

docs.title: States and verbs
docs.text:
State start stop / kill restart run <cell> delete Pending refused stops tasks; Stopped refused refused removes the cell Ready refused while a workload runs Stopped + OperatorStopped stop, then start attaches removes the cell Degraded recreates the cell Stopped + OperatorStopped recreates the cell recreates, then attaches removes the cell Stopped starts the existing containers stays Stopped starts starts, then attaches removes the cell Exited starts the existing containers stays Exited; any leftover task is ended starts starts, then attaches removes the cell Error recreates the cell stays Error with its reason; any leftover task is ended recreates the cell recreates, then attaches removes the cell Failed recreates the cell Stopped recreates the cell recreates, then attaches removes the cell Unknown refused stops tasks; Stopped refused refused removes the cell

Notes on the table:

  • start, restart and run <cell> share one decision in the daemon: Pending and Unknown are refused with a kuke delete cell pointer; Failed, Error and Degraded are recreated (stop, recreate the containers, start); Stopped and Exited, and a Ready cell whose tasks are gone, start from their existing container records. restart stops first only when the cell is Ready.
  • stop and kill differ only in the first signal (SIGTERM, escalating to SIGKILL after the timeout, versus SIGKILL straight away). Either verb ends and deletes every task in the cell, including tasks that had already exited, and waits (bounded) for each one to exit. Afterwards every container reads Stopped with its last exit code (137 for a SIGKILLed task).
  • The label after stop / kill is decided before anything is torn down. A Ready cell whose workload has already exited (for example kuke run --rm killing the cell after the workload finished) becomes plain Stopped without OperatorStopped, so the reconciler can still settle it to Exited and auto-delete it.
  • delete stops any task still running and removes the cell's containers, snapshots, cgroup and metadata.

docs.title: State diagram
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Stopped: kuke create cell
    Stopped --> Ready: start / run / restart
    Exited --> Ready: start / run / restart
    Ready --> Degraded: a workload crashed or is restarting
    Degraded --> Ready: workload back up
    Degraded --> Error: restart budget exhausted (wind-down)
    Ready --> Exited: all workloads exited 0 (wind-down)
    Ready --> Error: a workload exited non-zero (wind-down)
    Ready --> Error: root died (workloads killed)
    Degraded --> Error: root died (workloads killed)
    Ready --> Stopped: stop / kill (OperatorStopped)
    Degraded --> Stopped: stop / kill (OperatorStopped)
    Exited --> Exited: stop / kill (label kept)
    Error --> Error: stop / kill (label kept)
    Error --> Ready: start / run / restart (recreate)
    Degraded --> Ready: start / run / restart (recreate)
    Failed --> Ready: start / run / restart (recreate)
    Exited --> [*]: --rm auto-delete
    Stopped --> [*]: delete
    Exited --> [*]: delete
    Error --> [*]: delete
    Failed --> [*]: delete

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
# Materialise a cell from a daemon-stored CellBlueprint (containers declared in the Blueprint)
sudo kuke create cell mycell --from-blueprint web --realm main --space default --stack default

# Or apply a full cell manifest (preferred)
sudo kuke apply -f cell.yaml

# List cells
sudo kuke get cells --realm main --space default --stack default

# Start / stop / kill (positional — no `cell` subcommand)
sudo kuke start mycell --realm main --space default --stack default
sudo kuke stop  mycell --realm main --space default --stack default
sudo kuke kill  mycell --realm main --space default --stack default

# Delete (removes the cell and its materialised containers as a single unit)
sudo kuke delete cell mycell --realm main --space default --stack default

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• Container — what runs inside a cell
  • Stack — the parent of cells
  • Networking — how cell IPs and bridges work

docs.title: cgroups
docs.text: Kukeon mirrors its resource hierarchy into the Linux unified cgroup v2 tree. Every realm, space, stack, cell, and container has a corresponding cgroup. Policies applied at one level are inherited by everything below it — standard cgroup semantics.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
Everything Kukeon creates is rooted at /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon:

/sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/
├── main/                               <- realm
│   ├── default/                        <- space
│   │   └── default/                    <- stack
│   │       └── hello-world/            <- cell
│   │           ├── hello-world_root/   <- root container
│   │           └── web/                <- non-root container
│   └── monitoring/                     <- another space
└── kukeon-system/                      <- system realm
    └── kukeon/
        └── kukeon/
            └── kukeond/
                └── kukeond_root/

Each path segment is exactly the resource name (or <cell>_root for the root container of a cell).

docs.title: Why one cgroup per layer
docs.text:
• Realms can enforce or observe policy for every container in a tenant: a single memory.max on /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/<realm> caps the whole realm.
  • Spaces can carve out per-application resource envelopes.
  • Stacks group related cells under a single limit.
  • Cells are where co-located containers share limits.
  • Containers are the leaf where containerd actually attaches the OCI process.

You can apply cgroup knobs (cpu.weight, memory.max, io.max, etc.) at any level and they behave exactly as cgroups v2 specifies.

docs.title: Inspecting state
docs.text:
# Memory usage for a realm
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/main/memory.current

# CPU stats for a cell
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/main/default/default/hello-world/cpu.stat

# List processes in a container
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/main/default/default/hello-world/hello-world_root/cgroup.procs

docs.title: Creating policies
docs.text:
Kukeon does not yet expose cgroup policies as first-class fields on the manifest (memory.max on a realm, for example, is on the roadmap). In the meantime, you can write directly to the cgroup files. They persist across reconciles — Kukeon only creates missing directories; it does not clear values you set.

# Cap the main realm at 4 GiB
echo 4G | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/main/memory.max

Caveats:

  • cgroup values you set by hand are not reflected in kuke get.
  • They survive reboots only if you re-apply them (cgroups are a runtime concept).
  • When a realm is deleted, the cgroup directory is removed and any policies go with it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Kukeon needs the cgroup v2 unified hierarchy. On most modern distros this is the default. To check:

mount | grep cgroup2

If you see cgroup (v1) mounts instead, enable v2 on the kernel command line (systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1) and reboot.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• Realm — top-level cgroup parent
  • Space — space-level cgroup
  • Stack — stack-level cgroup
  • Cell — cell-level cgroup

docs.title: Client and daemon
docs.text:
Kukeon ships as a single binary that behaves as either kuke (client CLI) or kukeond (daemon) depending on the name it's invoked as. Installing Kukeon creates a hard link so both names resolve to the same on-disk binary.

/usr/local/bin/kuke     -> kukeon binary
/usr/local/bin/kukeond  -> same binary (hard-linked), different argv[0]

cmd/main.go inspects filepath.Base(os.Args[0]) and dispatches to the matching cobra tree. See Architecture → Process Model for the dispatch itself.

docs.title: kuke — the client
docs.text: kuke is the user-facing CLI. It does not directly own containerd, CNI, or cgroups; instead, it sends requests to kukeond over a unix socket. Every kuke subcommand — init, apply, create, get, delete, start/stop/kill, purge, refresh — is a client of the daemon by default.

docs.title: kukeond — the daemon
docs.text:
kukeond is a single long-lived process that:

  • listens on /run/kukeon/kukeond.sock (configurable via --socket);
  • serves the kukeonv1 API to every kuke client;
  • holds the containerd client, the CNI manager, and the cgroup manager;
  • reconciles desired state (from manifests) against actual state (in containerd, CNI, cgroups).

It runs as the root container of the kukeond cell inside the system realm, so it's managed by the same primitives as any other workload.

docs.title: In-process mode
docs.text:
kuke can bypass the socket and execute the operation in-process — but only for the commands that route through the promotable client. After #566/#588 the true workload verbs (apply, create *, run, attach, delete *, kill *) route through the daemon-only client, which ignores kukeon/noDaemon: for them neither KUKEON_NO_DAEMON=true nor --run-path reaches an in-process branch, and they always require the daemon.

The in-process path stays reachable for the surviving promotable callers — get *, purge *, log, refresh, restart, start, stop, doctor cgroups, plus the bootstrap commands init and uninstall. Reach it via:

  • --no-daemon directly, on the commands that carry the flag (init, uninstall, purge, every get <kind>), or
  • KUKEON_NO_DAEMON=true in the environment, or
  • an explicit --run-path /some/path (which auto-promotes to in-process mode — the daemon ignores client-supplied run-paths, so a caller passing a non-default --run-path would otherwise silently read/write the daemon's path instead).

--no-daemon stays accepted on kuke init, kuke uninstall, kuke purge, and every kuke get <kind> (the get kinds were retained per a user override on the original #222 AC so the in-process escape hatch stays available for every resource lookup, not just get realm). kuke image * is daemon-independent by design (always in-process regardless of any of these knobs).

# Surviving promotable caller via env var
sudo KUKEON_NO_DAEMON=true kuke get cells --realm default --space default --stack default

# Surviving promotable caller via --run-path promotion
sudo kuke purge realm myrealm --cascade --force --run-path /opt/kukeon

# Commands that still expose --no-daemon directly
sudo kuke get realms --no-daemon
sudo kuke get cells --no-daemon --realm default --space default --stack default
sudo kuke purge realm myrealm --cascade --force --no-daemon

When to use it:

  • Bootstrapping — kuke init runs in-process by necessity; the daemon isn't up yet.
  • Daemon is down — anything that should talk to kukeond but can't because the daemon is stopped or being rebuilt.

Trade-offs:

  • In-process mode requires root (it talks directly to containerd, netlink, cgroups).
  • There's no long-lived state holder, so every command is self-contained.
  • Two in-process commands running at the same time will race on the same on-disk state. Don't do it.

docs.title: The --host flag
docs.text:
The client talks to the daemon over a unix socket by default:

--host unix:///run/kukeon/kukeond.sock   (default)

Other transports are on the roadmap (ssh://user@host is the intended future shape), but today only the unix transport is supported. If you need to manage a remote host, bring your own tunnel — e.g. ssh -L /tmp/kukeond.sock:/run/kukeon/kukeond.sock user@host and then kuke --host unix:///tmp/kukeond.sock ….

docs.title: Parity between daemon and in-process
docs.text: kuke get realms and kuke get realms --no-daemon should return identical output on a healthy host. Divergence between them is a regression — if you see it, please file a bug. The two paths share the same reconciler and data store; the only difference is who holds the process. The explicit-flag check survives on every kuke get <kind> after #222 (get realm is the one the AGENTS.md dev-init regression guard exercises; the others are available as the same shape of escape hatch); #223 retires get realm's parity-check role once kuke status (#202) absorbs the parity contract.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• System realm — where kukeond runs
  • Process model — how argv[0] dispatch works

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text:
A connector is a kind of access a cell needs: the login of its harness, a token for an API, the identity it clones, pushes and signs with, the credential a Realm pulls private images with. An identity is one stored Secret that fills a connector — a subscription token, a work GitHub token, a bot's SSH key.

Connectors separate three decisions that used to be one:

Decision Made by Where it lives Which connectors a cell requires the role and its harness components of the blueprint and the Config Which identity fills each one by default the operator, once Realm, Space or Stack spec.defaults Which identity one team or one cell uses the team (connectors) or --connector the Config's fill, or the cell's provenance

So a token is stored once, picked by name, and replaced in one place.

Trusted network only

kuke serve — the web UI and its /api/connectors endpoints — has no authentication, and it can be bound to any address. Anyone who reaches it can create identities, change defaults and start cells that use them. Run it on a trusted network or loopback only. Secret material is write-only everywhere: no CLI verb, API response or error prints it.

docs.title: The connectors kuke ships
docs.text: Each connector is one file under team/connectors/<name>/connector.yaml.

docs.title: claude
docs.text:
How a Claude Code cell authenticates. The three methods exclude each other; kuke team enables exactly one on every claude Config.

Method Component Delivery Identity login claude-login the harness state volume none — log in once from an interactive cell subscription claude-subscription CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN opaque Secret: a token from claude setup-token api-key claude-api-key ANTHROPIC_API_KEY opaque Secret: an Anthropic API key, billed per token

login is the default: it is what a cell did before connectors existed. A subscription token is valid for a year and serves every role, so it is the method to choose when cells of several roles — or a headless task with an empty state volume — must start authenticated.

docs.title: codex
docs.text:
How a Codex cell authenticates. Same shape: one method per codex Config.

Method Component Delivery Identity login codex-login the harness state volume none — codex login from an interactive cell api-key codex-api-key OPENAI_API_KEY opaque Secret: an OpenAI API key access-token codex-access-token CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN opaque Secret: a Codex access token (Business and Enterprise plans)

docs.title: github
docs.text: GitHub API access for the gh CLI: one method, token, delivered as GH_TOKEN through the github-token slot, with the gh image capability. The token is never a git credential — clone, push and signing use the git connector.

docs.title: git
docs.text:
The identity a cell clones, pushes and signs with. A git identity is one ssh-key, basic-auth or opaque Secret that also carries readable facts:

Field Type Meaning hosts list Hosts or URL prefixes the Secret authenticates (github.com); required for ssh-key and basic-auth author Name <email> Commit author committer Name <email> Committer; git falls back to the author sign commits, tags What to sign with the key (ssh-key only) allowedSignersRef secret reference Allowed-signers file used to verify (ssh-key only)

git.identityRef names such a Secret — on a Realm, Space or Stack default, on a Config's git block, or on one repo's git. When a cell is rendered the daemon expands it into author, committer, one credential per host and, for an SSH key, signing with the same key. A field written next to the reference wins over the identity's, so a Config can keep the identity's key and credentials and state its own author. The rendered cell never carries the reference, only the result.

A role with needs.repos requires the connector. It is optional for the cell to start: a public repository clones without an identity.

docs.title: Author-only identities
docs.text:
An opaque git identity is author-only: it carries author (required) and committer, and no key. hosts, sign and allowedSignersRef are rejected on it. Its stored value is the fixed placeholder kukeon:git-author-only, which nothing reads. It is for a user without an SSH key who still wants commits made under their name.

  • A cell whose default names it gets the author and committer, no credential and no signing.
  • Named on one repo's git.identityRef, it sets that repo's author and no credential.
kuke create secret me --connector git --type opaque --author 'Me <me@example.com>'

--type opaque may be left out: --connector git without --type and without --from-file creates an author-only identity. With --from-file, --type is required. An author-only identity takes no value: --from-literal and --from-file fail with an author-only git identity stores no value; use --type ssh-key for a key.

docs.title: kuke connector
docs.text:
kuke connector manages git identities and Realm defaults from the command line:

kuke connector list                      # identities and Realm defaults
kuke connector import git --default      # store your SSH key and gitconfig author, make it the default
kuke connector default git git-ssh       # make an existing identity the Realm default
kuke connector default git --clear       # remove it

import git reads the SSH key and the global git configuration of the user running it. With a key it stores an ssh-key identity (git-ssh); without one, an author-only identity (git-author). It turns signing on only when user.signingkey names the imported key. See the git credentials guide.

docs.title: Import from host in the web UI
docs.text:
On the Connectors page, the git connector's Identities panel has an Import from host action. It takes a realm, the hosts, an optional identity name, an optional key and passphrase file, and a Make it the Realm default checkbox (on by default). It calls POST /api/connectors/git/import with {realm, hosts, name, key, passphraseFile, makeDefault} and runs the same import as kuke connector import git.

The import runs as the user running kuke serve: it reads that account's ~/.ssh and global git configuration. Under a service manager that may not be your shell account; the result shows the home directory and the key path that were read. The key and passphrase file are paths inside that home directory (.ssh/id_ed25519 or ~/.ssh/id_ed25519); absolute paths and .. are refused. Key material never appears in a response or an error. kuke serve has no authentication: see the Trusted network only warning at the top of this page.

The identity create form also offers opaque for git, with no value field: an author-only identity.

docs.title: registry
docs.text: The credential a Realm pulls private images with: a basic-auth Secret in the Realm, bound to a registry server by a spec.registryCredentials[] entry's secretRef. It is a Realm concern and never appears on a Config. See Private registry.

docs.title: Identities
docs.text:
An identity is a Secret tagged with its connector:

# A token identity
sudo kuke create secret work-github --connector github --from-file ./token

# A git identity: the key plus the readable facts
sudo kuke create secret bot-key --connector git --type ssh-key \
    --from-file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 \
    --author 'Dev Bot <bot@example.com>' --hosts github.com --sign commits,tags

--connector validates the Secret against the connector: its type must be one the connector accepts, required fields must be set, and each value must read as its declared type. Every field of the connector is a flag of its own (--author, --hosts, …) and can also be written --identity FIELD=VALUE.

$ sudo kuke get secrets -o wide
NAME         TYPE     CONNECTOR  REALM    SPACE  STACK  CELL  IDENTITY
bot-key      ssh-key  git        default  -      -      -     author=Dev Bot <bot@example.com>; hosts=github.com; sign=commits,tags
work-github  opaque   github     default  -      -      -     -

The tag and the fields are readable; the material never is. A Secret without a tag still works wherever it is named by hand — one created before connectors existed needs no migration — but a Secret tagged for one connector is refused for another.

docs.title: Defaults and precedence
docs.text:
The identity of a connector is resolved when a cell is rendered, most specific first:

  1. the cell's own choice (--connector),
  2. the Config's fill,
  3. the Stack default,
  4. the Space default,
  5. the Realm default.

A default is a spec.defaults.secrets entry keyed by the connector's slot (for git, spec.defaults.git.identityRef):

apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Realm
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  namespace: default.kukeon.io
  defaults:
    secrets:
      github-token:
        secretRef: { name: work-github, realm: default }
    git:
      identityRef: { name: bot-key, realm: default }

Defaults are live: a Config that chose no identity has no fill, so changing the default changes the identity of every such Config's next cell, with nothing to re-render. kuke team relies on this — it writes a Realm default for a slot only when no Realm, Space or Stack default exists yet, and never overwrites one.

$ sudo kuke get configs -o wide
NAME                  ...  CONNECTORS
kuke-majordomo-claude ...  claude=login, github=work-github (realm)
team-dev-codex        ...  codex=login, git=bot-key (config), github=MISSING

A required connector with no identity at any level is unresolved. Previewing or creating a cell from that Config fails with an error naming the connector; the web UI shows a Needs connector badge on the Config, counts the affected Configs on the Connectors page, and disables Create until a default is set or an identity is picked. A named identity that is missing, tagged for another connector or of the wrong type is an error even for an optional connector.

docs.title: Teams
docs.text:
A team picks a method and an identity per connector in its kind: Team file or its TeamEntry; a role entry overrides the team for that role.

apiVersion: kuketeams.io/v1
kind: Team
metadata:
  name: backend
spec:
  connectors:
    claude: { method: subscription, identity: claude-team }
    github: { identity: work-github }
    git: { identity: bot-key }
  roles:
    - name: reviewer
      source: agents
      path: roles/reviewer
      connectors:
        github: { identity: review-github } # this role only
  • method picks one of the connector's methods; empty selects its default.
  • identity names the Secret, name[@realm[/space[/stack]]]; without a scope it is looked up in the team's realm. Empty leaves the identity to the defaults.
  • A role entry that names no method keeps the team's method, and the team's identity unless it names its own. One that names a method states the whole choice.
  • A role entry also gives the role's cells a connector the role does not ask for itself.

Every rendered Config lists all its connector components under spec.components — the harness's auth method, git when the role works on repositories, and each connector the role or the team asks for. Only an identity the team chose is written as a fill on the Config; everything else stays with the defaults. A team's git identity is written on the Config (spec.git.identityRef), never on the Stack, because other teams share the Stack.

Roles written before connectors existed keep rendering: a role that lists the old secret names (claude-code-oauth-token, anthropic-api-key, openai-api-key, gh-token) selects the method that delivers that secret. Two such names of one connector are alternatives — the first method wins and kuke team says so; set connectors.<name>.method to choose.

docs.title: Per-cell overrides
docs.text:
sudo kuke create cell --from-config team-dev-claude --connector github=other-github
sudo kuke run -c team-dev-claude --connector git=release-key@ops
sudo kuke create cell --from-config team-dev-codex --connector-method codex=api-key --connector codex=my-openai-key

--connector <connector>=<secret>[@realm[/space[/stack]]] uses another identity for this one cell. The override is recorded in the cell's provenance (spec.provenance.connectorOverrides), so kuke restart and a reconcile-driven recreate render the cell with the same identity, and kuke create cell --clone carries it over. The flag is valid with --from-config only. An unknown connector, a missing Secret, or a Secret tagged for another connector is rejected before anything is created.

--connector-method <connector>=<method> uses another method of a connector for this one cell — for example a codex Config on login started once with api-key. The blueprint already carries every method of the connector as one exclusive group, so the cell enables the picked method's component in place of the one the Config enables; the Config itself is not changed. The new method's identity resolves as usual: a --connector override, the Config's fill, then the Stack, Space and Realm defaults — a Config's fill for its own method's slot does not carry over. The choice is recorded in spec.provenance.connectorMethods and kept by kuke restart, a reconcile-driven recreate and --clone. A connector the blueprint declares no methods for, a method it does not declare, or a connector the Config does not require (a method pick swaps a method, it never adds a connector) is rejected. Valid with --from-config only.

In the web UI's New Cell flow every required connector is pre-selected with its effective method and identity. A connector with several methods offers a method picker; choosing another identity or method sends the same overrides, and the preview shows the methods and identities the cell will use. A per-cell pick is allowed on a team-owned Config too: only the Config's own page shows its identities read-only, because kuke team add re-renders it.

docs.title: Why login volumes are not shared across roles
docs.text:
The login methods keep the session in the harness state volume, and that volume is per role — kuke-majordomo-claude and team-dev-claude each log in once. Sharing one volume across roles is deliberately not supported:

  • The state directory also holds the role itself — settings, skills and instructions the role's launch installs there — so a shared volume would let one role's content overwrite another's.
  • A Codex login's refresh token is single-use. Two cells refreshing one copied login invalidate each other.

When several roles must start authenticated without an interactive login each, use a token method instead: a Realm-default claude-subscription identity authenticates every claude cell, interactive or headless, with an empty state volume.

docs.title: Adding a connector
docs.text:
A connector is data. Adding one is one file, team/connectors/<name>/connector.yaml; no Go and no TypeScript names a connector, and a test (pkg/team/connector/guard_test.go) enforces it.

apiVersion: kuketeams.io/v1
kind: Connector
metadata:
  name: example-token # must match the directory
spec:
  title: Example
  description: An API token for the example service.
  scopes: [realm, space, stack]
  identity:
    secretTypes: [opaque]
    fields:
      - name: account
        required: true
        help: Account the token belongs to.
  methods:
    - name: token
      default: true
      delivery: env
      description: A token delivered as EXAMPLE_TOKEN.
      requires: [example-cli]
      secret:
        name: example-token
        envName: EXAMPLE_TOKEN

With that file the connector appears in kuke create secret --connector, team connectors, kuke create cell --connector, and the web UI's Connectors page and pickers.

Field Meaning title, description Display name and what the access is for identity.secretTypes Secret types accepted: opaque, basic-auth, ssh-key identity.fields[] Readable identity fields: name, type (string, list, person, secret), required, enum, secretTypes, help scopes Where a default may be set: realm, space, stack (empty allows all) harness The harness this connector authenticates; kuke team enables exactly one method on each of its Configs group Exclusion group of the method components (defaults to the connector's name) optional A cell may start without an identity methods[] The ways to deliver the connector; exactly one is default: true methods[].component Blueprint component name; <connector>-<method> when empty methods[].delivery env, file or stateVolume methods[].requires Image capabilities the method needs methods[].secret The slot: name, and envName (env) or an absolute mountPath (file); secretName and aliases for older roles delivery (no methods) git or registry: a connector delivered by a handler

Component names and slot names are unique across the catalog.

docs.title: Delivery handlers
docs.text:
The delivery says how an identity reaches a cell:

Delivery What it does env The Secret's value is set as the environment variable of the method's slot file The Secret's value is mounted read-only at the slot's path stateVolume Nothing is delivered: the login lives in the harness state volume git git.identityRef is expanded into author, committer, credentials and signing registry The Secret is the pull credential of a Realm's registryCredentials[] entry

env, file and stateVolume need no code. git and registry are the two handlers implemented in the daemon (internal/connector/handlers.go names their fields); a new connector with one of the first three deliveries is only a file.

The daemon keeps no catalog. kuke team copies each connector's definition into the blueprint component that requires it, so the daemon validates and resolves identities from the blueprint alone — including for a connector added after the daemon was built.
