docs.text:
• Secret manifest — spec.connector and spec.identity
  • Blueprint contract — components and groups
  • Teams — roles, harnesses and bindings
  • Git credentials — what a git identity expands into
  • Private registry — the registry connector

docs.title: Container
docs.text: A container is a plain OCI container, created and run by containerd, that belongs to a specific cell. Containers are the only layer in the hierarchy that corresponds directly to something you would recognize from Docker.

docs.title: What a container is
docs.text:
Creating a container materializes:

  1. An OCI container in containerd, in the realm's namespace (kukeon-<realm>).
  2. A cgroup leaf — /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/<realm>/<space>/<stack>/<cell>/<container>_<role> — where <role> is root for the root container or the container id otherwise.
  3. Metadata at /opt/kukeon/<realm>/<space>/<stack>/<cell>/containers/<container>.yaml.

The rootfs, image layers, and image content all live in containerd — Kukeon does not re-implement any of it. You can inspect the containerd-level state at any time:

sudo ctr -n kukeon-main containers ls
sudo ctr -n kukeon-main tasks ls

docs.title: Container spec
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Container
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  id: web
  realmId: main
  spaceId: default
  stackId: default
  cellId: hello-world
  root: true
  image: docker.io/library/nginx:alpine
  command: /bin/sh
  args:
    - -c
    - "exec nginx -g 'daemon off;'"
  env:
    - "NGINX_HOST=example.com"
  ports: []
  volumes:
    - source: /srv/html
      target: /usr/share/nginx/html
      readOnly: true
  networks: []
  networksAliases: []
  privileged: false
  restartPolicy: ""

See Manifest Reference → Container for the complete schema and the semantics of every field.

docs.title: Root vs. non-root containers
docs.text:
• Exactly one container in a cell is the root. Set spec.root: true in the manifest, or let Kukeon pick the first container if none is explicit.
  • The root container's network namespace becomes the cell's network namespace.
  • Non-root containers inherit the network namespace from the root. They do not get their own IP; they share the cell IP.
  • If the root container exits, the cell's network namespace goes away. Non-root containers should be designed to exit too.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: State What it means Pending Container metadata exists; containerd container not yet created Ready Task is running Stopped Task record exists but its task is gone, with no exit info (e.g. reaped post-reboot) Exited Task exited 0 — a clean completion (#1267) Error Task exited non-zero — a crash (#1267) Paused Task is paused (cgroup-frozen) Pausing Task is in the process of being paused Failed A kukeon container bring-up fault (reserved for kukeon's own faults — a non-zero task exit is Error) NotCreated No containerd record at all Unknown Daemon can't determine state

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Containers are not CLI-managed subjects on their own — they are not addressable by the CRUD or lifecycle verbs (create, delete, purge, start, stop, kill, restart); those operate on cells. Containers are declared inside a cell manifest and materialised as a side effect of the cell's lifecycle:

  • Declare containers inline under spec.cell.containers[] in a kind: Cell, kind: CellBlueprint, or kind: CellConfig manifest. Apply with kuke apply -f cell.yaml or run with kuke run -f cell.yaml / kuke run --from-config <cfg>.
  • Inspect the resulting runtime containers with kuke get container, tail logs with kuke log --container <name>, and open a session with kuke attach --container <name>.
  • Lifecycle is cell-level: kuke start <cell>, kuke stop <cell>, kuke kill <cell>, and kuke restart <cell> bounce every container in the cell as a single unit. There is no per-container start/stop/kill verb.
  • Removal of a single container is done by editing the manifest and re-applying (or re-running) the cell — kuke apply -f reconciles container sets, and the cell-level kuke delete cell tears down the whole cell including its containers.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• Cell — the parent of a container
  • containerd namespaces — where containers actually live
  • cgroups — the resource-control side

docs.title: containerd namespaces
docs.text: Kukeon doesn't run its own container runtime. It drives containerd, and every containerd operation it performs is scoped to a containerd namespace.

docs.title: The mapping
docs.text:
Realm containerd namespace main kukeon-main kukeon-system kukeon-system mytenant kukeon-mytenant (or whatever spec.namespace says)

By default, each realm's namespace is kukeon-<realm-name>. The realm manifest can override this via spec.namespace.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Containerd namespaces are the tenancy boundary. They scope:

  • Images — an image pulled into kukeon-main is not visible from kukeon-mytenant; each realm maintains its own image cache.
  • Containers — a container running in kukeon-main can only be listed, stopped, or inspected by a client scoped to kukeon-main.
  • Tasks — running tasks are namespaced too.
  • Snapshots and content — the underlying layer store is shared, but the references are namespaced.

This is also what lets Kukeon coexist with Docker or nerdctl on the same host. They use their own namespaces (moby, default, etc.) and never see Kukeon's.

docs.title: Inspecting state with ctr
docs.text:
Anything Kukeon does through containerd is visible to ctr, the low-level containerd CLI:

# Images in the main realm
sudo ctr -n kukeon-main images ls

# Containers in the main realm
sudo ctr -n kukeon-main containers ls

# Running tasks (the equivalent of `docker ps`) in the main realm
sudo ctr -n kukeon-main tasks ls

# Attach to a task's stdout (useful for debugging)
sudo ctr -n kukeon-main tasks attach <container-id>

If ctr -n <ns> images ls returns empty, the image was never imported into that namespace. A common cause is importing into default instead of the realm's namespace. See Build from source for the correct way to import.

docs.title: The system namespace
docs.text: kuke init creates a second realm, kukeon-system, with containerd namespace kukeon-system (or kuke-system.kukeon.io in older layouts). That's where the kukeond image lives. See System realm.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• Realm — the Kukeon-level tenant boundary
  • System realm — the dedicated realm for kukeond

docs.title: Networking (CNI)
docs.text: Kukeon uses the reference CNI plugins to give each space a network. There is nothing magic happening; Kukeon writes a conflist to disk and then invokes the CNI plugins the normal way when a cell's network namespace is set up.

docs.title: The shape of a space network
docs.text:
One space → one CNI network → one Linux bridge → one IP range.

Concretely, when you create a space:

  • Kukeon writes a CNI conflist at /etc/cni/net.d/<realm>-<space>.conflist (path configurable via spec.cniConfigPath).
  • The conflist references the bridge plugin with a bridge name derived from the space (see below).
  • The host-local plugin is used for IPAM.
  • On first cell creation, the kernel bridge appears on the host as a regular ip link show interface.

For the out-of-the-box main/default space, the bridge sits on 10.88.0.0/16.

docs.title: Bridge names and the 15-character limit
docs.text:
Linux interface names have a hard 15-character limit (IFNAMSIZ - 1 = 15). Kukeon's default bridge naming scheme — kuke-<realm>-<space> — can blow past that on long names:

kuke-main-default        # 16 chars, too long

Kukeon truncates safely before creating the bridge, using a stable hashing scheme so the same (realm, space) pair always produces the same bridge name. The CNI conflist records the actual bridge name that was used, and the daemon reads it back rather than recomputing.

docs.title: Recovering from a stale conflist
docs.text:
Older Kukeon versions computed bridge names without the safe-truncation rule. If you upgrade with a stale conflist on disk, the next kuke init or cell creation can fail with:

failed to attach ... to network: plugin type="bridge" failed (add):
failed to create bridge "kuke-...-...": could not add "...":
numerical result out of range

numerical result out of range is the kernel's ERANGE for "this interface name is too long." Fix:

sudo kuke init --force-regenerate-cni

That flag rewrites every space's conflist with the current naming scheme.

See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Cell-level networking
docs.text:
Inside a cell, only the root container has a network namespace — every other container joins it. So:

  • Each cell has exactly one IP on the space's bridge.
  • localhost inside any container in the cell reaches every port bound by any container in the cell.
  • Two cells in the same space can reach each other at the IP layer.
  • Two cells in different spaces cannot reach each other unless a container explicitly joins both networks.

docs.title: Inspecting network state
docs.text:
# List bridges
ip link show type bridge | grep kuke

# Show the conflist for a space
cat /etc/cni/net.d/main-default.conflist

# Find the pid of a cell's root container (from containerd) and peek into its netns
ROOT_PID=$(sudo ctr -n kukeon-main tasks ls | awk '/<cell>_root/ {print $2}')
sudo nsenter -t "${ROOT_PID}" -n ip -4 addr
sudo nsenter -t "${ROOT_PID}" -n ip route

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• Space — owns the network
  • Cell — gets one IP on the bridge

docs.title: The Kukeon hierarchy
docs.text:
Kukeon's resource model is a single, explicit hierarchy. Every container on a Kukeon host belongs to exactly one path through this tree:

flowchart LR
    Realm --> Space --> Stack --> Cell --> Container

Each layer maps to a concrete Linux primitive. There are no hidden layers and no "virtual" concepts that only exist inside the daemon.

Layer Linux primitive What it gives you Realm containerd namespace Tenant boundary Space CNI network + cgroup subtree Network and resource isolation Stack cgroup subtree Logical grouping within a space Cell Network namespace (one root container owns it) Pod-like co-location Container OCI container via containerd The actual workload

docs.title: Why five layers?
docs.text:
Docker has one layer (the container). Kubernetes has many (namespaces, workloads, services, ingress, nodes, pods). Kukeon sits between: enough layers to carve real isolation boundaries on a single host, but few enough that each one has a single, clear job.

  • Realm answers whose containers are these? — one realm per tenant, environment, or user.
  • Space answers what can they talk to? — each space is one CNI bridge, one IP range, one cgroup subtree for quotas.
  • Stack answers which cells are part of the same deployment? — groups related cells together for lifecycle operations.
  • Cell answers which containers share a network namespace? — like a Kubernetes pod, one unit of co-located containers.
  • Container answers what is actually running? — a plain OCI container.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
Say you are running two projects on the same host: a WordPress blog and a personal monitoring stack.

Realm: main
├── Space: blog          (CNI: 10.88.0.0/16)
│   └── Stack: wordpress
│       ├── Cell: wp
│       │   ├── Container: php-fpm
│       │   └── Container: nginx
│       └── Cell: db
│           └── Container: mariadb
└── Space: monitoring    (CNI: 10.89.0.0/16)
    └── Stack: observability
        ├── Cell: prometheus
        │   └── Container: prometheus
        └── Cell: grafana
            └── Container: grafana

The blog stack and the monitoring stack are on different CNI bridges, different cgroup subtrees, but share the same realm (one containerd namespace). If you wanted them fully isolated — different tenants, different registry credentials — each would get its own realm.

docs.title: System realm
docs.text: In addition to the realm you create, kuke init creates a second realm called kukeon-system. It is where the kukeond daemon itself runs, and it's managed by kuke the same way any other realm is. See System realm.

docs.title: The default hierarchy
docs.text:
When you run kuke init with no arguments, Kukeon creates:

  • A user realm default (containerd namespace kukeon-default)
  • A space default inside the default realm (CNI network default-default, bridge kuke-default-de… truncated to fit the 15-char kernel limit)
  • A stack default inside default/default
  • The system realm kukeon-system with the kukeond cell

Everything is idempotent. Re-running init reports already existed for the parts it finds on disk.

docs.title: Read next
docs.text:
• Realm — tenant boundary
  • Space — network + cgroup isolation
  • Stack — logical grouping
  • Cell — pod-like unit
  • Container — OCI workload
  • Client and daemon — how kuke and kukeond cooperate

docs.title: Realm
docs.text: A realm is the outermost layer of the Kukeon hierarchy. It is the tenant boundary: everything a realm owns is invisible from another realm, by construction.

docs.title: What a realm is, on disk and in the kernel
docs.text:
Creating a realm materializes three things on the host:

  1. A containerd namespace — all containers the realm runs live in a dedicated containerd namespace, named kukeon-<realm> by default. Images pulled into one realm are not visible from another.
  2. A cgroup subtree — /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/<realm> — used as the root for every space and stack inside the realm. This gives you a single place to attach quotas or account usage across the realm.
  3. Metadata at /opt/kukeon/<realm>/realm.yaml (under the run path, which is configurable via --run-path). This is the authoritative record that the realm exists; the daemon reconciles state from it.

docs.title: Realm spec
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Realm
metadata:
  name: main
  labels: {}
spec:
  namespace: kukeon-main
  registryCredentials: [] # optional, per-registry

The full schema is in Manifest Reference → Realm.

Key fields:

  • metadata.name — the realm's name, used everywhere as the realmId.
  • spec.namespace — the containerd namespace. Defaults to the realm name (or kukeon-<name> when bootstrapped by kuke init); you can set it explicitly.
  • spec.registryCredentials — a list of registry logins for images this realm pulls. Scoped to the realm: two realms can use the same image reference with different credentials.

docs.title: Realms and containerd namespaces
docs.text:
Every containerd operation Kukeon performs is scoped to a namespace. If you want to inspect what a realm sees, use ctr with the same namespace:

# List images in the `main` realm
sudo ctr -n kukeon-main images ls

# List running tasks (containers) in the `main` realm
sudo ctr -n kukeon-main tasks ls

Inspecting a different namespace (or no namespace) will not show anything Kukeon created for main. This is the main mechanism that gives realms their tenancy guarantee.

docs.title: Why you might want more than one realm
docs.text:
• Environments — dev, staging, prod as three realms on the same host.
  • Tenants — one realm per user or project on a shared host.
  • Registry credentials — different teams pull from different private registries.
  • Accounting — one cgroup subtree per realm makes it easy to bill or enforce quotas.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
# Create
sudo kuke create realm mytenant --namespace kukeon-mytenant

# Get (list)
sudo kuke get realms

# Get (single, as YAML)
sudo kuke get realm mytenant -o yaml

# Delete (with --cascade to remove children)
sudo kuke delete realm mytenant --cascade

See CLI Reference → create, get, delete.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• containerd namespaces — how the realm/namespace mapping works
  • cgroups — the realm's cgroup subtree
  • System realm — the special kukeon-system realm

docs.title: Space
docs.text: A space is one step inside a realm. It owns one CNI network and one cgroup subtree. Everything that needs to share a layer-2 segment or a pool of compute resources lives in the same space.

docs.title: What a space is, on disk and in the kernel
docs.text:
Creating a space materializes:

  1. A CNI configuration file at /etc/cni/net.d/<realm>-<space>.conflist (by default). The conflist points at the bridge and host-local plugins and owns the space's IP range.
  2. A Linux bridge on the host, named kuke-<realm>-<space> (truncated if needed — see Networking). Every cell in the space gets a veth pair into this bridge.
  3. A cgroup subtree — /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/<realm>/<space> — parent of every stack and cell cgroup in the space.
  4. Metadata at /opt/kukeon/<realm>/<space>/space.yaml.

docs.title: Space spec
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Space
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  realmId: main
  cniConfigPath: /etc/cni/net.d # optional; defaults to system CNI dir

The full schema is in Manifest Reference → Space.

docs.title: Network boundary
docs.text:
Everything inside the same space can reach everything else inside the same space by default, at the IP layer. Two cells in two different spaces cannot reach each other unless you explicitly connect them (typically by having a container join both networks).

This is Kukeon's primary network-isolation knob. If you want firewalling between groups of cells, put them in different spaces.

docs.title: cgroup boundary
docs.text:
The space cgroup is the parent of every stack cgroup in the space, which in turn is the parent of every cell's cgroup. A quota or limit set on the space cgroup is inherited by everything underneath.

/sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/main/default/         <- space cgroup
├── stackA/
│   ├── cell1/
│   │   └── cell1_root/                      <- root container
│   └── cell2/
└── stackB/

This gives you a single, reliable place to put CPU/memory/IO limits that apply to an entire space.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
# Create a space inside the main realm
sudo kuke create space mySpace --realm main

# List spaces in a realm
sudo kuke get spaces --realm main

# Delete (with --cascade to remove child stacks, cells, containers)
sudo kuke delete space mySpace --realm main --cascade

docs.title: Bridge name length limit
docs.text: Linux limits interface names to 15 characters (IFNAMSIZ - 1). Kukeon's bridge name scheme, kuke-<realm>-<space>, can exceed that for long names. Kukeon truncates safely before creating the bridge, but if an old conflist on disk has a too-long name from before the fix, re-run kuke init --force-regenerate-cni to regenerate it. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• Networking (CNI) — how the CNI side of a space works
  • cgroups — the full cgroup tree
  • Realm — the tenant that owns the space
  • Stack — what lives inside a space

docs.title: Stack
docs.text: A stack is a logical grouping of related cells. Stacks don't add a network boundary — the space does that — but they do add their own cgroup subtree and serve as a naming scope for cells that belong to the same deployment or application.

docs.title: What a stack is
docs.text:
Creating a stack materializes:

  1. A cgroup subtree — /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/<realm>/<space>/<stack> — parent of every cell in the stack.
  2. Metadata at /opt/kukeon/<realm>/<space>/<stack>/stack.yaml.

That's it. A stack has no network configuration of its own.

docs.title: Stack spec
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Stack
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  id: default
  realmId: main
  spaceId: default

See Manifest Reference → Stack for the full schema.

docs.title: When to create a new stack
docs.text:
A stack is the right boundary when you want:

  • A group of cells you'll deploy, stop, or tear down together.
  • A cgroup subtree you can apply compound resource limits to (for example, a limit that covers a whole application's cells but not the rest of the space).
  • A namespace for cell names — two stacks in the same space can both have a cell called web without colliding.

If you don't need any of that, keep using the default stack.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
# Create a stack inside main/default
sudo kuke create stack myapp --realm main --space default

# List stacks in a space
sudo kuke get stacks --realm main --space default

# Delete (with cascade to remove child cells)
sudo kuke delete stack myapp --realm main --space default --cascade

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• Space — the network + cgroup parent of a stack
  • Cell — what lives inside a stack
  • cgroups — the full cgroup tree

docs.title: System realm
docs.text:
kuke init creates two realms, not one:

  • A user realm — default by default — for your workloads.
  • A system realm called kukeon-system for Kukeon's own infrastructure.

The system realm is where kukeond runs.

docs.title: What lives there
docs.text:
On a freshly bootstrapped host:

Realm: kukeon-system
└── Space: kukeon
    └── Stack: kukeon
        └── Cell: kukeond
            └── Container: kukeond_root   (image: ghcr.io/eminwux/kukeon:<version>)

The kukeond daemon runs as the root container of the kukeond cell, inside a dedicated cell → stack → space → realm path. This means:

  • The daemon is managed by the same primitives as your workloads — cgroups, containerd namespace, CNI network.
  • Tearing it down uses the same kuke commands you'd use for any other cell.
  • Upgrading the daemon is just "swap the image and recreate the cell."

docs.title: Why a separate realm?
docs.text:
• Tenancy — the system realm is isolated from your workload realms. A user realm going sideways (or being removed) doesn't touch the daemon.
  • Accounting — kukeond's CPU and memory usage roll up under /sys/fs/cgroup/kukeon/kukeon-system, separate from your applications.
  • Lifecycle — kuke can manage the daemon the same way it manages anything else; there's no "special path" for the system cell.

docs.title: Operating the system realm
docs.text:
You can inspect it with the same commands:

$ sudo kuke get cells --realm kukeon-system --space kukeon --stack kukeon
NAME     REALM            SPACE    STACK    STATE   ...
kukeond  kukeon-system    kukeon   kukeon   Ready

Stopping or restarting the daemon:

sudo kuke kill kukeond        --realm kukeon-system --space kukeon --stack kukeon --run-path /opt/kukeon
sudo kuke delete cell kukeond --realm kukeon-system --space kukeon --stack kukeon --run-path /opt/kukeon
sudo rm -f /run/kukeon/kukeond.sock /run/kukeon/kukeond.pid

In-process mode is required because the daemon itself is what's being stopped — kuke has to talk to containerd directly. An explicit --run-path (or KUKEON_NO_DAEMON=true) promotes the command into in-process mode.

See Guides → Init and reset for the full teardown-and-bootstrap loop.

Older layouts

On earlier versions of Kukeon, the system realm used kuke-system.kukeon.io as the containerd namespace. kuke-system and kukeon-system refer to the same concept depending on which version you bootstrapped the host with.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• Realm — the realm concept in general
  • Client and daemon — how kuke and kukeond cooperate

docs.title: Teams
docs.text:
A team is a set of agent cells composed from roles (what an agent is told to do) and harnesses (which agent CLI runs it, in which image). For every selected role × harness pair, kuke team renders one CellConfig — the pair's answers — against a shared CellBlueprint, applies them to kukeond, and records the accepted declaration on the host. Composing a team never creates or starts cells: launch them explicitly, for example with kuke run --from-config <team>-<role>-<harness>.

Two commands drive it:

  • kuke team init creates the global configuration and applies the kuke team, whose one role is majordomo. kuke is the operator's reserved system team; add refuses that name.
  • kuke team add composes a project team from a directory's kuketeam.yaml or from a named Git source.

docs.title: Where the files live
docs.text:
File Where Holds ~/.kuke/kuketeams.yaml host TeamsConfig, optional and hand-written: global defaults (sources, roles, harnesses), parameters, secret bindings. ~/.kuke/kuketeam.d/<team>.yaml host TeamEntry: the accepted declaration of one registered team. Written only after a fully successful apply. kuketeam.yaml project repo Team: the project's selections, read by kuke team add DIRECTORY. roles/<role>/ a source Role definition (role.yaml) and the instruction/skill assets materialized into the harness home. harnesses/<harness>/ a source Harness definition (harness.yaml), image catalog (images.yaml), and image build context.

All documents use apiVersion: kuketeams.io/v1 and are decoded strictly (single document, no unknown fields). This repository ships the majordomo role under team/roles/ and the claude, codex, opencode, and script harnesses under team/harnesses/ (script runs a program role, see Program roles); other roles (dev, pm, pr-reviewer, …) can come from any Git source, such as the agents repository. The kukeon renderer that turns a pair into kukeon documents is embedded in kuke (pkg/team/compose/renderers/kukeon/v1beta1); see team/harnesses/templates.md for the harness and renderer contract.

docs.title: Selections and persistence
docs.text:
TeamsConfig.spec.defaults and Team.spec share sources, roles, and harnesses. An omitted list inherits the corresponding global default. An explicit list replaces it; [] selects none. References are checked against the effective lists. Each source has exactly one of branch, tag, or commit. A role with an explicit harness selects only that harness, and fails if the role does not declare it; otherwise it selects every harness in the effective list that the role declares in spec.harnesses, and fails only if it declares none of them. A team can therefore list [claude, script] and keep agent roles that declare only claude. Harness default is not supported; use roles[].harness. Unselected definitions are neither fetched, loaded, nor rendered.

apiVersion: kuketeams.io/v1
kind: Team
metadata:
  name: example
# All selections omitted: inherit the operator's defaults.

A TeamEntry has the same metadata and spec as the accepted Team, plus the projectSource that kuke team add resolves. Effective defaults are not persisted, and omitted versus explicit-empty lists round-trip unchanged, so a later recomposition picks up the current global defaults.

Authored roles[].needs.image contains capability names, never image URLs. These additions cannot erase requirements in Role.spec.needs.image. The selected harness is also a mandatory image capability. One catalog image must satisfy the complete set; catalog order breaks ties, and a root-capable image is not selected unless root is requested. The team name root grants no privilege. Published image references are read from the images.yaml beside the selected harness.yaml; no registry lookup is made. An update re-resolves the image from the current definitions and catalog.

docs.title: Reusable defaults after init
docs.text:
~/.kuke/kuketeams.yaml is optional and hand-written: kuke reads it and never writes it, and a missing file means empty global defaults. kuke team init and kuke team add both work without it. Create it to declare reusable sources, roles, and harnesses. Both harnesses are listed here; dev narrows to Claude and pm to Codex:

apiVersion: kuketeams.io/v1
kind: TeamsConfig
spec:
  defaults:
    sources:
      - name: kukeon
        url: github.com/eminwux/kukeon
        branch: main
      - name: agents
        url: github.com/eminwux/agents
        branch: main
    roles:
      - name: dev
        source: agents
        path: dev
        initialPath: /home/user/work
        harness: claude
      - name: pm
        source: agents
        path: pm
        initialPath: $HOME
        harness: codex
    harnesses:
      - name: codex
        source: kukeon
        path: team/harnesses/codex
      - name: claude
        source: kukeon
        path: team/harnesses/claude

Check external role paths, runtime clonePath requirements, image capabilities, and secret prerequisites against the selected source revision before use.

docs.title: Starting directory
docs.text:
initialPath is accepted on role selections in global defaults, Team, and TeamEntry. An explicit roles list replaces the entire global list, so omitting initialPath on a replacement role uses the home fallback rather than borrowing a path from the same-named global role.

Supported values are clean absolute Unix paths (including /), $HOME, and $HOME/subdirectory, with path components of letters, digits, _, ., and -. Relative paths, ~, ${HOME}, other variables, shell expressions, whitespace, empty strings, and ./.. components are rejected. Omit the field to start in the in-cell harness user's $HOME. $HOME resolves to the renderer profile's HOME (/home/user), never the host HOME. Directories must already exist; a failed cd stops startup before the harness runs.

initialPath controls startup even when a role declares the project repository slot. To start in the project, set initialPath to the project's absolute in-cell clone destination. Role path still locates definition assets: materialization runs against the role source before launch and installs instructions and skills in the harness's native home directories.

docs.title: Shared blueprints
docs.text:
A blueprint rendered by kuke team is a form with no role facts in it, so it is shared: one blueprint per harness × security profile, realm-wide, used by every role and every team in the realm — and by the web UI's New config form. See Blueprint contract.

Blueprint For roles that need <harness> the default posture (claude, codex, opencode) <harness>-root the root image capability: a privileged cell with a nested container runtime <harness>-host the kukeond-socket and kuke-binary host mounts <harness>-root-host both

A role that selects any other set of host mounts — only one of the two, or kukeon-install as well — gets a profile named after them, such as <harness>-kuke-binary-kukeon-install-kukeond-socket. The security posture is fixed in the blueprint and is never a Config toggle.

The daemon socket and the kuke binary are mounted through directories, so a daemon restart or a rebuild reaches running cells without recreating them:

Selector Mounted kukeond-socket /run/kukeon/kukeond/, where kukeond hard-links its socket on every start; the cell's KUKEON_HOST points at /run/kukeon/kukeond/kukeond.sock kuke-binary /opt/kukeon/bin/client/ at /.kukeon/client/, where kuke init stages its own binary, and a fixed shim at /usr/local/bin/kuke that runs it; re-run kuke init after a rebuild kukeon-install /opt/kukeon, read-only

Each blueprint is assembled from components: the harness (its parameters, env, secret slots and start modes, copied from harness.yaml), and the optional connector and forge components of the library kuke ships under team/components/ (github, github-issues). Everything that differs between two roles lives in the pair's CellConfig:

Role fact In the CellConfig Image picked for the role's needs.image values.IMAGE, plus requires for the capabilities Role source checkout, role path, start dir values.ROLE_SOURCE_DIR, ROLE_PATH, INITIAL_PATH Harness settings (claude settings file, codex sandbox/approval, opencode permissions) values.HARNESS_SETTINGS, SANDBOX, APPROVAL, PERMISSIONS Repositories repos.role-source, repos.project, one slot per further cloned source Secrets secrets.<slot> → a stored Secret Connectors and forges components Harness state volume values.STATE_VOLUME

Blueprints carry kukeon.io/shared: "true" and no team label. One realm has one copy of each shared blueprint: when a team renders different content under a shared name, its apply replaces the blueprint in place, whichever teams' Configs reference it, and says so in a note (old → new content digest, and the other Configs using it). Their cells turn OutOfSync and pick up the new content on kuke restart. The last apply wins, so keep teams on the same harness revision by pinning it in each team's sources. Only a blueprint kuke team did not render — without the shared label — is never overwritten; this team's is then applied as <name>-<content digest>. A team's apply removes a shared blueprint it stopped using only when no other CellConfig references it.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
A harness declares the ways it starts under spec.modes in harness.yaml — the shipped ones declare interactive and headless. The mode is picked per cell, so one role Config serves both:

kuke run acme-dev-claude                                               # interactive
kuke run acme-dev-claude --mode headless --param PROMPT="triage #42" -d

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
A role can declare named tasks in role.yaml: unattended runs that need no runtime arguments. Each task names one of the role's skills by base name, and can add a fixed argument string:

# role.yaml
spec:
  skills: [dev/skills/pick-issue, dev/skills/pick-changes]
  tasks:
    - { name: pick-issue, skill: pick-issue }
    - { name: pick-bug, skill: pick-issue, args: "--label bug" }
    - { name: pick-changes, skill: pick-changes }

A team's role entry picks which of them it uses. If tasks is omitted, the team gets all of the role's tasks. tasks: [] gives none, and a name the role does not declare fails kuke team add. A task whose skill is not one of the role's spec.skills also fails, with an error that names the role, the task and the skill.

# kuketeam.yaml
spec:
  roles:
    - { name: dev, source: agents, path: dev, tasks: [pick-issue, pick-bug] }

kuke team add renders each selected task as its own CellConfig per selected harness (the role entry's harness pin applies), named <team>-<role>-<harness>-<task> and labelled kukeon.io/task: <task> next to the team and role labels. It has the same blueprint, values, repos, secrets, components and requires as the pair's config, plus:

spec:
  modes: { enabled: [headless], default: headless }
  values:
    { PROMPT: "Use the pick-issue skill with arguments: --label bug", ... }
  autoDelete: true

The prompt is the same for every harness: Use the <skill> skill, followed by with arguments: <args> when args is set. Launch a task with no --rm and no --param. The cell deletes itself when the run ends:

kuke run -d acme-dev-claude-pick-bug

A harness without a headless mode gets no task configs, and the output says why. The pair's interactive config does not change. Tasks that need a value at run time (issue <N>) still go through it: kuke run --rm -d acme-dev-claude --mode headless --param PROMPT="work on issue 22". When a task is deselected, or the role stops declaring it, the next kuke team add prunes its config along with the team's other obsolete configs.

docs.title: Scheduling a task
docs.text:
A task config can run on a schedule instead of by hand. How often a task runs is a deployment decision, so the team sets it. An entry in a role's tasks is either a task name or an object that also gives the task's cadence:

# kuketeam.yaml
spec:
  roles:
    - name: dev
      source: agents
      path: dev
      tasks:
        - pick-issue # runs only when started by hand
        - { name: pick-bug, schedule: "*/15 * * * *" }
        - { name: pick-nits, schedule: "@daily", suspend: true }

schedule is a five-field cron expression or one of @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly, read in UTC. suspend: true keeps the schedule but switches it off.

A role can ship defaults for both, so a team that just names the task gets them:

# role.yaml
spec:
  tasks:
    - {
        name: pick-bug,
        skill: pick-issue,
        args: "--label bug",
        schedule: "*/30 * * * *",
      }
    - {
        name: health-sweep,
        skill: health-sweep,
        schedule: "@hourly",
        suspend: true,
      }

Each value a team's entry sets overrides the role's default for that value, and the other one is kept. The pick-bug entry above replaces the role's */30 * * * * with */15 * * * *. A role can ship a schedule that is off until a team opts in, as health-sweep does: the team turns it on with { name: health-sweep, suspend: false }. A suspend on a task that ends up with no schedule fails kuke team add, because there is nothing for it to switch.

kuke team add renders the resolved values into the task config's spec.schedule, and kukeond then fires the config on that schedule: each fire starts a <config>-<unix-fire-time> cell, and a fire is skipped while the previous one is still running. A task with no schedule renders as before. See what is scheduled, and when it next fires, with kuke get configs.

Team configs are re-rendered: kuke team add rewrites every one of them whole. A schedule or suspend edited by hand on a task config is therefore lost on the next kuke team add. Change it in kuketeam.yaml (or the role's defaults) instead.

A team's entry can also replace a task's argument text with args, for example { name: pick-bug, args: "--label regression" }. Like schedule and suspend, it overrides only that value.

docs.title: Program roles: the script harness
docs.text:
A role that is a plain program, such as a reactor or a poller, runs on the script harness. Its cell runs a command the role declares, with no model and no login, and gets the same connectors, repos, mounts and secrets as any other role:

# role.yaml
apiVersion: kuketeams.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: { name: ticker }
spec:
  harnesses:
    script:
      command: python3 "$ROLE_SOURCE_DIR/$ROLE_PATH/tick.py"
  connectors: [github]
  needs:
    mounts: [kuke-binary, kukeond-socket]
  tasks:
    - { name: tick, args: "--once", schedule: "*/5 * * * *" }
  • harnesses.script.command is required, and only the script harness accepts it. The cell runs it as /bin/bash -c "$COMMAND $ARGS" from the role's starting directory, and the cell exits with its status. Reference environment variables as $VAR, never ${VAR}: kukeon substitutes the braced form in blueprints, so kuke team add rejects it. The command is composed from the role; spec.parameters cannot override COMMAND.
  • Tasks take args and name no skill: a task config runs the command with the task's args appended (values.ARGS) instead of a PROMPT. schedule, suspend and the team's overrides work as for any task. A script task that sets skill fails kuke team add.
  • State. $SCRIPT_STATE_DIR (/home/user/.script-state) is on the pair's state volume, <team>-<role>-script-state, which the pair config and its task configs share, so the program keeps a small state directory across runs.
  • Assets. A program role's directory may hold only role.yaml: the script harness needs no AGENTS.md and loads no skills.
  • Image. The harness runs on the published ghcr.io/eminwux/kukeon/base-user image (bash, git, gh, jq, yq, python3); no harness image is built for it. base-user carries no io.kukeon.capabilities label yet, so kukeond logs image declares no capabilities; required capabilities not verified when it creates a script cell, and creates it.
  • Modes. There is only a headless mode; a script cell is not an attachable session.

kukeon's own kuketeam.yaml runs the agents repository's pipeline role this way: pinned to script, with tasks: [{ name: tick, suspend: false }] switching on the five-minute tick the role ships suspended. To stop the reactor:

  • Durably: set tasks: [{ name: tick, suspend: true }] on the role entry in kuketeam.yaml (or remove the role entry) and run kuke team add.
  • Immediately: kuke delete config kukeon-pipeline-script-tick. No new tick fires, and worker cells that are already running are left alone. The next kuke team add renders the config again.

docs.title: The majordomo health sweep
docs.text:
The kuke team's majordomo role declares one task, health-sweep, with schedule: "@hourly" and suspend: true. kuke team init therefore renders kuke-majordomo-<harness>-health-sweep suspended: no install spends model credits on sweeps until its user turns them on.

A sweep is read-only. It reads kukeond's health digest (kuke health), stops if the digest is clean, and otherwise triages each finding and stores one report in kukeond. It never restarts, deletes or changes anything; fixes appear in the report as suggested commands.

To turn sweeps on, edit the kuke team's stored entry and reapply it. The entry is the team's source: kuke team init writes it and kuke team init --reapply recomposes the team from it.

# ~/.kuke/kuketeam.d/kuke.yaml
spec:
  roles:
    - name: majordomo
      source: kukeon
      path: team/roles/majordomo
      initialPath: $HOME
      needs:
        image: [go]
      tasks:
        - { name: health-sweep, suspend: false }

kuke team init --reapply
kuke get config kuke-majordomo-claude-health-sweep -o yaml   # spec.schedule, status.schedule

Change the cadence the same way, with schedule: "*/30 * * * *" in the task entry. Run one sweep by hand at any time, suspended or not:

kuke run -d kuke-majordomo-claude-health-sweep
kuke health reports
kuke health report latest

The sweep cell deletes itself when it ends. It uses the same state volume as the interactive kuke-majordomo-<harness> config, so it runs with the harness login you made there.

docs.title: Filing kukeon defects as issues
docs.text:
By default majordomo has no GitHub access: a sweep only stores its report, and the interactive cell cannot search or file issues. GitHub access is opt-in per install, and a default kuke team init needs no GitHub token. One secret turns it on for both the interactive cell and the sweep:

  1. Create the token as a secret named gh-token:
kuke create secret gh-token --realm default --from-file /path/to/token
  1. In the kuke entry, give the role that secret, and tell the sweep where to file if it should:
# ~/.kuke/kuketeam.d/kuke.yaml
spec:
  roles:
    - name: majordomo
      # ...
      needs:
        image: [go]
        secrets: [gh-token] # enables the github connector: GH_TOKEN + gh
      tasks:
        - name: health-sweep
          suspend: false
          args: "--file-issues <owner>/<repo>"
  1. Run kuke team init --reapply.

needs.secrets in a team entry adds runtime secrets to a role for that team only; the role itself still requires none. gh-token enables the github connector, so the interactive kuke-majordomo-<harness> cell and its health-sweep task cell both get the token as GH_TOKEN and an image with gh. The token is never a git credential: clone and push keep using the git identity.

With the token, the sweep submits its report with kuke health report submit --file-issues <owner>/<repo>, and kuke does the filing: one issue per new kukeon finding, a comment on the open issue of a recurring one, and never anything for workload or unclear findings. See kuke health report submit for the issue format and what is redacted.

In the interactive cell, ask majordomo to file a defect it diagnosed. Its file-kukeon-bug skill looks for an existing issue first, sweep-filed ones included, then comments on it or opens one, and reports the URL. It renders the issue with kuke health issue, which uses the sweep's redaction and signature marker, so the two paths dedupe against each other. Without the opt-in it says filing is unavailable and how to turn it on.

Do step 1 before step 3, so the secret exists when the cells first start.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text:
A connector is a kind of access a cell needs. A role enables one by name:

# role.yaml
spec:
  connectors: [github] # GH_TOKEN for the gh CLI, plus the `gh` image capability
  forges: [github-issues] # optional; implies the github connector

The github connector's token is used only for the GitHub API. It is never a git credential: clone, push and signing use the git identity below. The older spelling — harnesses.<h>.secrets: [gh-token] with needs.image: [gh] — still composes and enables the same connector, filled from the same gh-token secret.

Two more connectors are enabled without the role asking: the one that authenticates the pair's harness (claude or codex — exactly one of its methods per Config, the login by default) and git, for a role with needs.repos.

A team decides how each connector is delivered and which identity fills it under connectors, in its kind: Team file or TeamEntry; a role entry overrides the team for that role and can give the role a connector it does not ask for itself:

# kuketeam.yaml (kind: Team) or ~/.kuke/kuketeam.d/<team>.yaml
spec:
  connectors:
    claude: { method: subscription, identity: claude-team }
    github: { identity: work-github }
    git: { identity: bot-key }
  roles:
    - name: reviewer
      # ...
      connectors:
        github: { identity: review-github }

identity names a stored Secret, name[@realm[/space[/stack]]]. A connector left out — or an entry with no identity — uses the default method and inherits its identity from the Stack, Space and Realm defaults, so replacing a default reaches every team that did not choose, with no re-render. Only identities a team chose are written as fills on its Configs. See Connectors → Teams for the full rules.

docs.title: Git identity and credentials
docs.text:
Team cells use stored git credentials; the host ~/.ssh is never mounted. A team cell's git identity is the git connector identity a Realm, Space or Stack default names (spec.defaults.git.identityRef), or the one the team names under connectors.git. kuke team reads no git identity from the host and writes no git defaults. Store yours with kuke connector import git --default.

TeamsConfig has no spec.git: a kuketeams.yaml that still has one fails to decode and names kuke connector import git --default. A source may state its own identity with sources[].git (author, committer, credential, signing); it is rendered into that repo's fill of each CellConfig. The remote transport follows the credential, so a project added by its HTTPS URL is still cloned and pushed over SSH when its host is bound to an SSH key.

When a team clones a source over SSH that states no credential of its own and nothing gives its cells a git identity, kuke team init and kuke team add print no git identity is set; run kuke connector import git --default. A role's needs.mounts: [ssh] is still accepted but mounts nothing.

docs.title: Runtime repository and parameter bindings
docs.text:
A source is the single declaration of its URL and branch/tag/commit. Optional sources[].clonePath requests a runtime clone at an absolute in-cell destination; omitting it requests no runtime clone. The initial kuke TeamEntry clones its role source to /home/user/kukeon-src.

The selected role's source and every Role.spec.needs.repos slot must resolve to an effective source with clonePath. Other effective sources with clonePath also request clones. Clone destinations must be unique. The github.com/owner/repo URL shorthand becomes HTTPS in runtime config fills; authored declarations keep their spelling.

The shared blueprint declares the repository slots role-source (the selected role's source) and project, plus one slot per further cloned source; destinations, URLs and revisions are bound through CellConfig values and spec.repos. Branches map to branch; tags and commits map to ref. The harness launchers preserve this checkout: they do not switch branches or pull newer revisions during launch.

TeamsConfig.spec.parameters is a string map of declared scalar parameters. Each composition binds only keys its blueprint declares. Required parameters without defaults must be supplied, and unknown keys fail. The parameters composition derives from the role and source selections (IMAGE, ROLE_PATH, STATE_VOLUME, …) cannot be set here. AGENT_NAME defaults to the full resource identity. Parameters must not hold credentials: use secret bindings instead.

A role declares the further parameters it reads in Role.spec.needs.params. Each entry is a bare name, which the operator must supply in TeamsConfig.spec.parameters, or a { name, default } mapping that carries the role's own value:

needs:
  params:
    - REGION
    - { name: AGENTS_REPO, default: "${ROLE_SOURCE_REPO}" }

A default may reference any composed fact as ${FACT}. Besides the values composition derives (ROLE_PATH, ROLE_SOURCE_DIR, …) there is ROLE_SOURCE_REPO: the <owner>/<repo> of the role source's URL, reduced from scp-like (git@host:owner/repo), ssh:// and https:// URLs with or without a trailing .git. A fork's roles therefore point at the fork without an edit. ROLE_SOURCE_REPO is a fact only: it is not a blueprint parameter and spec.parameters cannot set it.

The resolved value is written to the CellConfig and exported into the cell environment under the parameter's name. Precedence, highest first: TeamsConfig.spec.parameters.<NAME>, then the role's default, then the blueprint's empty default. A role cannot set a default for a parameter the blueprint or composition already declares (PROMPT, AGENT_NAME, IMAGE, …). When a URL does not reduce to <owner>/<repo> (a nested group path, a local path), ROLE_SOURCE_REPO is empty, and kuke team init / kuke team add print a note naming the role and each parameter whose default resolved empty.

Harness-owned onInit scripts (spec.onInit, or each mode's) call the image-installed /opt/kuketeams/harness/Makefile.start setup, which runs make -C "$ROLE_SOURCE_DIR" <harness> ROLE="$ROLE_PATH" against the role's checkout. A repository that serves roles therefore exposes one Makefile target per harness — this repository's make claude, make codex, and make opencode-openrouter (all backed by team/scripts/materialize-role.sh). Startup then uses INITIAL_PATH; the harness source need not be checked out in the cell.

The base majordomo clones over HTTPS and needs no git credential.

docs.title: Secret declarations
docs.text:
Only selected role/harness requirements contribute bindings. The shipped majordomo has no gh or gh-token requirement. Claude and Codex authenticate through their connector, by default with the login kept in the state volume, and declare no mandatory token. OpenCode's selected provider requires openrouter-api-key.

Each required secret is bound by name, in this order of precedence:

  1. the identity the team chose for the secret's connector (connectors, above);
  2. the binding recorded in the team's TeamEntry (~/.kuke/kuketeam.d/<team>.yaml secrets:), including any operator edit to it;
  3. a global TeamsConfig.spec.secrets binding;
  4. the default: the slot is left to the Realm → Space → Stack defaults.

A binding from 1–3 is written as a fill on the Config. The default is not: the Config carries no fill, and kuke team writes a Realm spec.defaults.secrets entry for the slot — pointing at the runtime secret of the same name in the team realm (gh-token, openrouter-api-key) — only when no Realm, Space or Stack default exists for it yet. It never overwrites one, so the default the operator sets later is the one every such Config uses.

A shared blueprint fixes where a secret lands: a harness slot (openrouter-api-key → OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and a connector slot (github-token → GH_TOKEN, claude-code-oauth-token → CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN) keep their declared destination, and a binding whose envName differs is rejected. A role secret no harness or component declares becomes an optional slot on the shared blueprint, with the binding's envName.

Composition records every binding the selected pairs use in the TeamEntry, so a repeated add or a recomposition from the entry alone keeps them. Bindings for requirements no selected pair uses are dropped. Because the recorded binding wins, change a binding after its first add by editing the TeamEntry (or delete it there to fall back to the global binding or default). A requirement whose name cannot yield an environment identifier (e.g. it starts with a digit) must be bound explicitly. The project's kind: Team file never declares bindings.

An explicit global binding looks like this:

# Optional, under TeamsConfig.spec (or the same shape under TeamEntry secrets).
secrets:
  - name: openrouter-api-key # identifier in Role.spec.harnesses.opencode.secrets
    secretRef:
      name: provider-account
      realm: auth
      space: shared
      stack: operators
    envName: OPENROUTER_API_KEY
    # Optional fallback if application finds no runtime secret:
    source:
      env: OPERATOR_OPENROUTER_KEY
      # Alternatively: file: /absolute/path/to/private/provider-key

name, the scoped secretRef, and envName are required. source is optional; when present it names exactly one environment variable or absolute file path — there is no inline value field. Composition emits secret references in configs and consumption slots in blueprints; it never reads values or emits Secret documents. Application checks runtime existence, reuses existing secrets, and reads a creation source only when a secret is missing.

docs.title: Resource names and state volumes
docs.text:
Pairs follow role order, then harness order. Each pair's config is named <team>-<role>-<harness>, with dots and punctuation runs collapsed to single hyphens: team esp32, role pr-reviewer, and harness codex produce esp32-pr-reviewer-codex. A task config appends the task name: esp32-pr-reviewer-codex-pick-review-pr. Different selections can collide on these readable names (root-a/majordomo and root/a-majordomo); choose distinct names in the same scope. Within one team, composition fails when two role × harness pairs produce the same config name (role a-b and role a.b), and the error names both pairs. kukeon.io/team labels keep the authored team name, and kukeon.io/role labels the role name from the team's roles list, on pair and task configs alike. Resources default to realm/space/stack default.

A harness keeps its state (logins, sessions) on a Volume named after the pair's config plus -state: <team>-<role>-<harness>-state, for example kuke-majordomo-claude-state or esp32-pr-reviewer-codex-state. The Volume is mounted only at the harness's statePath ($HOME/.claude for claude, $HOME/.codex for codex). It is not the cell's home or root filesystem, and a harness without a statePath gets no state volume. The pair config, its task configs and the sweep cell all mount the same one, so one harness login covers every cell of that role × harness.

The Config passes the name to the shared blueprint as STATE_VOLUME, and the Volume's scope as STATE_VOLUME_REALM, STATE_VOLUME_SPACE and STATE_VOLUME_STACK (the Config's own realm, space and stack). The blueprint mounts it through a fully-qualified volumeRef with ensure: true, so the first cell creates the Volume at those coordinates and the web UI links it.

Installs composed before this name existed used <team>-<role>-<harness>[-<project>-<role>-<harness>]-<digest>. Composition does not migrate those Volumes: after re-rendering, each role × harness starts with a new, empty state volume, so log in to each harness again. Delete the old Volumes with kuke delete volume once they are no longer needed.

docs.title: What preflight covers
docs.text: Preflight covers strict document shape, selection/reference resolution, role assets, template and partial execution, image capabilities, parameter completeness, repository bindings, and structural secret requirements. It does not prove published image availability, runtime scope or secret existence, source credentials, daemon acceptance, or live authentication; those surface when the team is applied or a cell is launched.

docs.title: Applying manifests
docs.text: kuke apply is the declarative interface: write a YAML file describing the resources you want, and Kukeon reconciles the host to match. It's the preferred way to create or update anything that isn't a one-off CLI operation.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
sudo kuke apply -f my-cell.yaml

Accepts a single path, or - to read from stdin:

cat my-cell.yaml | sudo kuke apply -f -

The manifest can contain one or more resource documents separated by ---:

apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Space
metadata:
  name: blog
spec:
  realmId: main
---
apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Stack
metadata:
  name: wordpress
spec:
  id: wordpress
  realmId: main
  spaceId: blog
---
apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: Cell
metadata:
  name: wp
spec:
  id: wp
  realmId: main
  spaceId: blog
  stackId: wordpress
  containers:
    - id: nginx
      image: docker.io/library/nginx:alpine

kuke apply creates resources in dependency order — parents (realm → space → stack) before children (cell → container), regardless of the order they appear in the file.

docs.title: What apply does
docs.text:
Per resource, the outcome is one of:

  • created — the resource didn't exist; it was created.
  • updated — the resource existed but its spec differs; it was reconciled. Printed diffs follow.
  • unchanged — the desired state already matches; nothing to do.
  • failed — reconciliation failed; the error is printed. Processing continues for other resources, and the command exits non-zero at the end.

Example output:

$ sudo kuke apply -f stack.yaml
Space "blog": created
Stack "wordpress": created
Cell "wp": created

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text:
sudo kuke apply -f my-cell.yaml -o json
sudo kuke apply -f my-cell.yaml -o yaml

With -o json or -o yaml, apply emits a structured report instead of the human-readable one.

docs.title: Idempotence
docs.text: apply is idempotent: running the same manifest twice is safe. The second run should report unchanged for every resource.

docs.title: Nesting and ordering
docs.text:
Today, each resource is a separate document. There is no "apply an entire stack as one tree" mode — you write the stack, then the cells under it, either in the same multi-doc file or separately.

Cross-file apply:

sudo kuke apply -f realm.yaml
sudo kuke apply -f space.yaml
sudo kuke apply -f stack.yaml
sudo kuke apply -f cell.yaml

or multi-doc:

cat realm.yaml space.yaml stack.yaml cell.yaml | sudo kuke apply -f -

docs.title: kuke apply always requires the daemon
docs.text:
kuke apply routes through kukeond and has no in-process fallback. After #566/#588 the workload verbs (apply, create *, run, attach, delete *, kill *) route through the daemon-only client, which ignores kukeon/noDaemon — so KUKEON_NO_DAEMON=true and the --run-path promotion do not reach an in-process branch for apply. If the daemon is down, bring it back with kuke daemon start (or kuke init from scratch) before applying.

The in-process escape hatch survives only for the promotable callers — get *, purge *, log, refresh, restart, start, stop, doctor cgroups, plus the bootstrap init/uninstall. See Client and daemon for the broader story.

docs.title: Parameterized cell blueprints
docs.text:
kuke apply -f consumes a fixed manifest — the file you ship is the spec the daemon reconciles to, with no substitution layer in between. When you need the same cell shape with different values per invocation (image tag, command, mount paths), apply a CellBlueprint to the daemon and run it with kuke run --from-blueprint instead of editing the YAML each time.

A blueprint is a daemon-stored, scoped resource. It declares its variable inputs alongside the cell template:

apiVersion: v1beta1
kind: CellBlueprint
metadata:
  name: shell
  realm: default
spec:
  parameters:
    - name: IMAGE
      description: container image to run
      default: alpine:latest
    - name: CMD
      description: command to exec
      required: true
  cell:
    containers:
      - id: shell
        image: ${IMAGE}
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "${CMD}"]

Apply it once:

sudo kuke apply -f shell.blueprint.yaml

Then kuke run --from-blueprint shell materializes one cell with a unique name (<prefix>-<6hex> by default, prefix = spec.prefix or metadata.name; override with --name) and resolves each ${KEY} reference in the body. Resolution order, highest first:

  1. --param KEY=VALUE on the CLI (repeatable)
  2. Values from --param-file <path> (one KEY=VALUE per line, # starts a comment)
  3. The parameter's default in the blueprint
  4. The kuke process env (os.LookupEnv)
  5. Required + unset → error; non-required + unset → empty string
# Use defaults / env / required errors
kuke run --from-blueprint shell --param CMD="echo hi"

# Override the image too
kuke run --from-blueprint shell --param IMAGE=alpine:edge --param CMD="/bin/sh"

# Load a batch of values from a file, with a CLI override on top
kuke run --from-blueprint shell --param-file ./shell.env --param IMAGE=alpine:edge

--param, --param-file, and --name are rejected when combined with -f (file mode is not a blueprint and has no parameter declarations); --param/--param-file are also rejected with --from-config (a CellConfig already binds its own values — use --env for a per-cell override there). The substituted body is what reaches the daemon — there is no parameter layer in the manifest API itself.

To additionally fill a blueprint's structural repo/secret slots, wrap it in a kind: CellConfig and use kuke run --from-config <cfg>; see kind: CellConfig. Both --from-blueprint and --from-config stamp a fresh <prefix>-<6hex> cell per invocation (pin one with --name).

See kuke run for the full flag surface.
